prompt: How does the section relate the enthalpy H to the constant-pressure heat capacity C_P?

choices.why: The temperature derivative of U at constant volume is C_V. C_P is the temperature derivative of H at constant pressure.
That is how H changes with pressure. C_P is how H changes with temperature, at constant pressure.
That is the inverse, 1/C_P. C_P is the slope of H against T at constant pressure.

explanation: C_P is the rate at which the enthalpy rises with temperature at constant pressure, ((∂H)/(∂T))_P. So H and C_P are related by differentiation, and H can be found from C_P by integration.

prompt: The section outlines a way to find the enthalpy H(T) from heat capacity data. What are its two steps?

choices.text: Measure C_P against T, then integrate it
Measure H against T, then differentiate it
choices.why: Differentiating H gives C_P, not H. The section measures C_P as a function of T and integrates it to get H(T).

choices.text: Measure C_P at one T, then multiply by T
choices.why: C_P changes with temperature, so one value is not enough. C_P must be measured over a range of T and integrated.

choices.text: Measure C_V against T, then integrate it
choices.why: H is linked to the constant-pressure heat capacity, C_P = ((∂H)/(∂T))_P. So it is C_P that is measured and integrated.

explanation: Because C_P = ((∂H)/(∂T))_P, measuring C_P as a function of temperature and integrating it gives H(T). The section then lists the problems with doing this.

prompt: The first problem the section lists with finding H by integrating C_P is the reference point. What is that problem about?

choices.text: Choosing the lower limit of the integral
Measuring C_P accurately enough
choices.why: The reference-point problem is not about precision. It is about where the integration starts, so that one compound can be compared with another.

choices.text: Choosing the units of the enthalpy
choices.why: Units are not the issue. The problem is the lower limit of integration, a starting point that lets compounds be compared.

choices.text: Choosing the upper limit of the integral
choices.why: The upper limit is just the temperature of interest. The trouble is the lower limit, the reference point where the integration starts.

explanation: Integrating C_P gives only the change in H from some starting temperature. Ideally the start would be zero kelvin, but it cannot be reached, so the question is how to compare one compound with another.

prompt: Ice at its melting point is heated slowly at constant pressure. According to the section, what happens to its temperature while it melts?

choices.text: It holds steady until the ice is gone
It rises steadily as heat is added
choices.why: While ice melts, the added heat goes into the heat of fusion, not into warming. The temperature rises only once all the ice is gone.

choices.text: It drops until all the ice is gone
choices.why: Adding heat does not cool the ice. The temperature stays at the melting point while the heat of fusion is absorbed.

choices.text: It rises, but more slowly than in water
choices.why: During melting the temperature does not rise at all. All the added heat goes into the heat of fusion until the ice is gone.

explanation: The heat of fusion must be added until all the ice has melted before the temperature can go up again. During that time heat flows in at a fixed temperature.

prompt: What happens to the enthalpy H of a substance at a phase transition, such as the melting of ice?

choices.text: It jumps suddenly
It drops to zero
choices.why: H does not vanish when a solid melts. It jumps up by the heat of the transition, here the heat of fusion.

choices.text: It stays the same
choices.why: Heat is absorbed at constant pressure during melting, so H rises. It jumps by the heat of fusion while T stays fixed.

choices.text: It rises smoothly with T
choices.why: During melting T does not change, yet H rises by the heat of fusion. That is a sudden jump, not a smooth rise.

explanation: At a phase transition the heat of transition is taken in with no change in temperature, so H jumps suddenly. These jumps are one of the problems with finding H by integrating C_P.

prompt: According to the section, what is C_P at a jump in H, such as at the melting point of ice?

choices.text: It is infinite
It is zero
choices.why: Heat goes in with no rise in temperature, so the slope (∂H)/(∂T) is not zero but infinite.

choices.text: It equals the heat of fusion
choices.why: The heat of fusion is the size of the jump in H, not C_P. Because H rises with no change in T, C_P is infinite there.

choices.text: It equals C_V
choices.why: The constant-volume heat capacity is not the point here. At the jump H rises with no change in T, so C_P = ((∂H)/(∂T))_P is infinite.

explanation: C_P = ((∂H)/(∂T))_P is the slope of H against T. At a phase transition H rises while T stays fixed, so the slope, and with it C_P, is infinite.

prompt: What does the section stress about absolute enthalpies?

choices.text: There are no absolute enthalpies
They come from integrating C_P from 0 K
choices.why: Zero kelvin cannot be reached, and integrating C_P gives only changes in H. The section stresses that there are no absolute enthalpies.

choices.text: They are tabulated for each compound
choices.why: What can be measured and tabulated are enthalpy changes, such as heats of fusion. There are no absolute enthalpies.

choices.text: They are always positive
choices.why: With no natural zero, H has no fixed sign. The section stresses that there are no absolute enthalpies, only changes in H.

explanation: Integrating C_P gives only the change in H from a starting point, and there is no natural zero for H. So there are no absolute enthalpies, which is why a reference point is needed to compare compounds.

prompt: At constant pressure, a sample's enthalpy rises by 750 J when it is warmed by 20.0 K. Taking C_P as constant over this range, C_P = ((∂H)/(∂T))_P ≈ ΔH/ΔT. What is C_P, in J/K? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: C_P ≈ ΔH/ΔT = 750 J/20.0 K = 37.5 J/K. C_P is the slope of H against T at constant pressure.

prompt: Ice at its melting point is heated at constant pressure, and all of it must melt before the temperature can rise. The heat of fusion of ice is 6.01 kJ/mol. How much heat must be added to melt 3.00 mol of ice, in kJ? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: q = 3.00 mol × 6.01 kJ/mol = 18.03 kJ. All of this goes in at the melting point with no rise in temperature, which is the jump in H.
